coverage_gaps: Need a region-by-region U.S. map of load growth and interconnection constraints across PJM, ERCOT, MISO, SERC, WECC, and NYISO before ranking public companies.
Need current company-level backlog, book-to-bill, and lead-time disclosures for electrical equipment vendors, transformer manufacturers, and grid EPC contractors.
Need utility IRP and rate-case evidence to determine whether grid capex benefits suppliers, regulated utilities, IPPs, or customers.
Need fuel-cycle contract evidence for uranium, conversion, enrichment, and HALEU rather than relying on uranium spot-price narratives.
Need gas-turbine order backlog, delivery-slot availability, and pipeline constraint data to separate commodity gas upside from equipment/EPC bottlenecks.
Need policy-risk review for renewables tax credits, nuclear incentives, LNG export approvals, FERC interconnection rules, and emissions regulations as of mid-2026.
Need market-pricing check in later layers: valuation, revenue exposure, margin expansion, and whether obvious beneficiaries are already crowded.

evidence.claim: IEA states that global electricity demand is expected to grow rapidly in 2025 and 2026, supported by industry, appliances, air conditioning, data centres, EVs, and other electrification drivers.
evidence.source_title: Global electricity demand to keep growing robustly through 2026 despite economic headwinds

evidence.claim: IEA Electricity 2026 frames the period as an 'Age of Electricity' with growing consumption from AI, data centres, electrification of industry, transport, and buildings, and includes focused analysis on grids and flexibility.
IEA Electricity 2026 says renewables, natural gas, and nuclear together are expected to meet all additional global electricity demand in aggregate over 2026-2030.

NERC's 2025 Long-Term Reliability Assessment highlights intensifying resource-adequacy risks over the next decade and notes that data-center projects have moved from speculative/exploratory stages into development commitments that affect load forecasting.
DOE's Office of Electricity states that distribution transformers are building blocks of the electric grid and are facing supply-chain constraints, long lead times, and component shortages.

DOE reports that COVID-era supply and labor constraints plus material shortages drove distribution-transformer lead times from three to six months in 2019 to 12 to 30 months in 2023, the latest available data cited on the DOE page.

FERC directed PJM to establish transparent rules to facilitate service for AI-driven data centers and other large loads co-located with generating facilities, while addressing reliability and capacity-addition concerns.
evidence.source_title: FERC Directs Nation’s Largest Grid Operator to Create New Rules to Embrace Innovation and Protect Consumers

evidence.claim: IEA's Gas Market Report Q1 2026 states that global LNG supply growth is set to accelerate in 2026, supporting stronger natural-gas demand and a new all-time high.

EIA's AEO2026 analysis projects U.S. dry natural gas production to increase significantly over coming decades, meeting growing domestic and international demand, and includes a case exploring higher power demand from data centers.
evidence.source_title: Domestic and international demand drive natural gas production growth

evidence.claim: DOE announced that Centrus produced about 900 kilograms of HALEU by June 2025, describing HALEU as a crucial fuel source needed by most advanced reactor designs.
evidence.source_title: Centrus Reaches 900 Kilogram Mark for HALEU Production

evidence.claim: World Nuclear Association states that HALEU will be needed for many advanced power reactor fuels and more than half of SMR designs in development.
IEA's Global Critical Minerals Outlook 2025 notes that expanding construction and electrification of grids and industrial equipment are fueling increased copper demand.
evidence.source_title: Overview of outlook for key minerals - Global Critical Minerals Outlook 2025

memory_update.text: Energy theme should be reframed as electricity-system expansion: AI/data centers plus electrification pull on grid equipment, dispatchable power, nuclear fuel, renewables/storage, and critical materials.
Grid transformers, substations, interconnection, and transmission EPC are likely first-pass Serenity chokepoints because they gate both new load and new generation.
Nuclear research should separate reactor announcements from fuel-cycle scarcity; HALEU enrichment and fuel fabrication may be a higher-quality bottleneck than speculative SMR deployment.
Gas exposure should be decomposed into commodity gas, LNG exports, pipelines, gas turbines, on-site data-center generation, and capacity-market economics.

Renewables and storage exposure should focus on interconnection-ready assets, storage integration, inverters, grid-forming controls, and curtailment economics rather than undifferentiated solar module supply.

Layer 1B should build a 30-60 company public-market universe across utilities, IPPs, electrical equipment, grid services, gas/LNG, uranium/fuel cycle, renewables/storage, and critical materials, then attach evidence strength and bottleneck scores.

layer1a.summary: Layer 1A decomposition: the Energy theme should be treated as an electricity-system expansion theme rather than a simple commodity call. The broad demand shock comes from AI/data centers, industrial reshoring, EV/building electrification, cooling demand, and global emerging-market load growth. The highest-quality Serenity chokepoint work should start with grid interconnection, transformers, transmission services, gas-fired dispatchable generation, nuclear fuel/enrichment, renewables-plus-storage integration, and critical materials. Public-market mapping should avoid starting from a single ticker and instead build universes around equipment lead times, regulated interconnection rules, qualified vendor lists, fuel-cycle scarcity, EPC capacity, and long-duration revenue visibility. This is research support only and not a buy/sell recommendation.

supply_chain_nodes.bottleneck_hypothesis: The investable bottleneck is not merely who consumes power; it is where large loads have committed projects that require firm power, rapid interconnection, and high reliability faster than utilities can build generation and wires.
supply_chain_nodes.node: AI/data-center and broad electrification load growth
supply_chain_nodes.public_asset_hunting_notes: Search for hyperscaler capex, utility load-growth disclosures, data-center campus permits, state economic-development filings, PJM/ERCOT/MISO/SERC load forecasts, and companies selling mission-critical electrical infrastructure rather than only cloud operators.

supply_chain_nodes.bottleneck_hypothesis: The chokepoint may be less the commodity gas molecule and more the deliverable system: turbines, interconnection, pipelines, air permits, capacity-market rules, LNG export ramp timing, and regional basis constraints.

supply_chain_nodes.bottleneck_hypothesis: The more defensible chokepoints may be grid-forming inverters, battery integration, utility-scale storage development, software/control systems, and interconnection-ready projects rather than commodity solar panels alone.

demand_drivers: AI and hyperscale data-center electricity demand, especially in U.S. regions with clustered interconnection requests.
Broad electrification of industry, transport, buildings, cooling, and appliances, which turns energy growth into electricity growth.
Grid reliability requirements as variable renewables, generator retirements, extreme weather, and large flexible or inflexible loads interact.
Need for firm, low-carbon, or lower-carbon power for corporate procurement, nuclear restarts/life extensions, SMRs, renewables, storage, and gas backup.
Global LNG and natural-gas demand from power-sector reliability needs, industrial demand, and LNG trade expansion.
Energy-security and domestic supply-chain policy support for nuclear fuel, grid components, transformers, and critical minerals.
theme_map.public_market_search_strategy: Build the research universe by node, not by ticker. First map demand owners such as hyperscalers, utilities, IPPs, industrial loads, and LNG buyers. Then map scarce suppliers: transformer OEMs, electrical-equipment vendors, grid EPC contractors, gas-turbine OEMs, gas producers/midstream/LNG exporters, uranium miners, converters/enrichers/fuel fabricators, reactor vendors, renewables developers, storage integrators, inverter suppliers, and copper/electrical-steel exposure. For each node, verify evidence with filings, utility IRPs, interconnection-queue data, FERC/NERC/DOE/EIA/IEA reports, capex plans, order backlog, lead-time commentary, plant permits, customer announcements, and margin/backlog quality. Downgrade companies whose exposure is narrative-only, whose bottleneck is not validated by orders/backlog, or whose economics are absorbed by regulated customers rather than suppliers.
supply_side_constraints: Transmission, interconnection, substation equipment, and distribution-transformer lead times can gate the pace of load connection even when generation is available.
Large power transformers, distribution transformers, electrical steel, copper, EPC labor, and grid services capacity are practical expansion chokepoints.
Dispatchable generation additions face gas-turbine lead times, pipeline constraints, permitting, emissions policy risk, and capacity-market uncertainty.
Advanced nuclear faces long licensing/construction timelines plus fuel-cycle constraints, especially HALEU enrichment, conversion, fabrication, and qualification.
Renewables and storage face interconnection queues, curtailment risk, inverter/grid-forming requirements, battery mineral supply, and local permitting.
Oil and gas remain tied to power reliability through gas-fired generation, LNG export demand, fuel security, drilling/service capacity, and midstream availability.
